name: IBM / Carbon
era: Contemporary design system · authored web adaptation
idea: A strict grid and precise typography make substantial workflows manageable and data easy to compare.
origin: Carbon is IBM’s open design system. Its productive typography supports tasks with forms, controls and dense information. Expressive typography creates space for editorial moments. This demo uses an authored compact project workspace with IBM Plex Sans.
tip: Organize data around the actual task. Use compact typography for work and larger headings where they establish orientation.

finder.signature: IBM Plex, rectangular actions and a structured data table.

strengths: A strict grid and precise typography make substantial workflows manageable and data easy to compare.
A documented system supports consistent component decisions.
risks: High density must not displace field labels, readable spacing or helpful error messages.
These colors, sizes and radii describe this demo, not a full vendor token specification.
The web adaptation does not reproduce native window management, assistive technology integration or device input.
a11y: Test visible keyboard focus, screen-reader names, 200% text resizing and contrast in every state. Use system colors for native implementations and retain text labels for status. These editorial scores are not an accessibility certification.
longevity: Stable hierarchy and task structure outlast individual theme generations. Check current platform components when implementing.
verdict: A strict grid and precise typography make substantial workflows manageable and data easy to compare. Organize data around the actual task. Use compact typography for work and larger headings where they establish orientation.

platforms.web: Authored HTML/CSS comparison; use semantic controls in a product.
platforms.mobile: The table becomes a single-column list with labeled metadata. Rectangular surfaces and IBM Plex remain; fields and actions grow to touch size.
platforms.desktop: The broad reference shows the system’s task hierarchy. Actual native applications also need platform navigation and input conventions.
